speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: Mr Chairman, I beg to move, "That the total sum to be allocated for Head W of the estimates be reduced by $100".

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: Technological disruptions and our changing economic and social needs are the main drivers of this.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: New Mass Rapid Transit (MRT) lines and stations are being built in many places.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: Private hire cars and their distinct blue decals ply our roads.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: There is a proliferation of e-bikes, personal mobility devices (PMDs) and shared bicycles on our roads and pathways.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: Our once bustling port in Keppel has gone silent as the move to Tuas continues.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: Changi Airport has transformed from its humble beginnings to an international air travel hub of four terminals with a fifth one in the works.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: And it is absolutely vital that we do so!

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: Our transport industry is a key pillar and enabler of our economy.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: It not only connects us domestically within Singapore but also to the rest of the world.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: However, rapid evolution and major changes in transport have brought about its own set of challenges and issues.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: Private hire car companies leverage technology through their mobile apps to plug a service gap by providing a platform to efficiently match private hire car drivers and passengers directly in real time and space.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: Technology has also brought about new options for first- and last-mile travel between our homes and the various transport nodes.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: These include e-bikes and PMDs and also bike sharing systems.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: I expressed reservations about the proliferation of e-bikes and PMDs during the Active Mobility Debate.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: Bike sharing systems, while intuitively an efficient and convenient option for Singaporeans to use for short distance travel, face teething issues, such as abusive use and abandonment of the shared bikes.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: I shall not delve too much into these details as they have been well-documented in the mass media and many of my hon colleagues on both sides of the House will raise the same during this COS.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: An important point to note, however, is that new technologies will continue to disrupt and bring new options into the transportation industry.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: Further technology-driven changes in transport are already at our doorstep.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: Driverless, autonomous vehicles are being tested and piloted.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: Difficulties and problems arising from these will not be dissimilar or unique.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: This does not mean that we ignore the difficulties and problems.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: They are real and should never be trivialised.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: Policy solutions need to be urgently found to solve or mitigate the issues.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: The question we should ask ourselves, Sir, is this.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: Should the Government hesitate to promote technological changes in transport and maintain the status quo because of these difficulties and problems?

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: I think that the clear answer is a clear no.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: Stifling new innovative technology can only end in a negative outcome for the overall Singapore economy and for Singaporeans in general.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: We did not get where we are as a country by being fearful of the difficulties and problems that change will bring.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: It is perhaps an understatement to say that it has been a difficult year for our MRT system and for Singapore Mass Rapid Transit (SMRT) in particular.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: Some minor, others of a serious nature that need to be addressed immediately.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: The signalling system on old lines is being upgraded to increase efficiency and to cope with increased demand.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: This is in line with our population growth and new towns and housing estates being developed.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: Such problems and difficulties arising from the evolution and changes in the transport industry is not unprecedented.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: It has happened many times in the past.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: Public housing, town planning, port facilities, Changi Airport, roads and our first MRT system each presented similar difficulties and problems at its time.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: Each of these was meticulously planned, executed with vision and foresight by our founding leaders.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: They were policies implemented not only to satisfy the current requirements of its time but also to cater for the potential needs in the future.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: The choice of location and the anticipation of our future needs set the foundations for the possibility of the state-of-the-art multi-terminal international airport that we have today.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: The same vision is being applied today in the relocation of our port facilities to Tuas, the massive expansion of our MRT lines and the entire array of car-lite initiatives to alter our transportation landscape in the future.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: Transport is an indelible part of the everyday life of Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: On any given day, Singaporeans potentially utilise and come into contact with private hire cars, taxis, buses, the MRT, PMDs, e-bikes, cyclists on bikes and shared bikes.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The previous Transport Minister, Mr Lui Tuck Yew, had indicated that some growth in car numbers was required to meet the aspirational needs of car-owning Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In line with the Government’s move towards a car-lite Singapore and the newly implemented zero-growth car and motorcycle policy, these changes have also provided new opportunities to review fundamental assumptions, beliefs and policies towards vehicle ownership in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Decades ago, Mr Lee Kuan Yew revealed that Singapore’s water security made every other policy bend at the knee.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Today, raising the total fertility rate (TFR) is important, if not critical for Singapore.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Smaller families have added mobility needs that are particularly acute when children are young, from birth to around 12-16 years of age.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: No doubt, there are some families with young children who may not need a car.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: But each family's circumstances can be very different.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Would the Ministry look into this prospect to support families with young children in particular?

speaker: The Chairman
text: You have six minutes, you have two cuts.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: First, I declare my interest as the Executive Secretary of the National Transport Workers' Union (NTWU).

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: BCM has benefited bus captains tremendously, as they now earn salaries that are almost equal to the national median wage, and enjoy better benefits and working conditions.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: New bus depots and interchanges are now designed with the welfare of our bus captains and station staff in mind, and these are very much appreciated by our bus workers.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Mr Chairman, BCM did not just benefit bus captains.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Under BCM, public bus operators are incentivised for good service reliability and reduced bus bunching.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Can MOT provide an update on the performance of the respective public bus operators?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Have they met their key performance indicators (KPIs) under BCM?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Are there any plans by the Land Transport Authority (LTA) to further tighten these KPIs?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: How much incentives have been paid out to the operators since the introduction of BCM?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I ask because, ultimately, the ones who are tasked to fulfil these KPIs are our bus captains.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: With BCM, our bus captains have had to adapt to new performance indicators, and this has added new pressures to an already challenging job.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Fatigue can occur in all industries but numerous studies have focused its effects on shift workers and drivers, and our bus captains are both shift workers and drivers.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: The union hopes to have the support of LTA and our public bus operators to conduct a joint fatigue study of our bus captains.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: This would allow us to identify stress points and work together on early interventions.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: However, the existing bus depots and interchanges, especially the older ones, were not designed to accommodate the increased number of buses.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Can MOT provide an update on the plans for new depots and interchanges, and if there are any plans to upgrade existing ones?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I do hope that LTA will continue to work with the union to factor in worker-centric designs when building new bus facilities or upgrading the old ones.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: To drive these new buses, the operators hired hundreds of new bus captains who are trained at the Singapore Bus Academy.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Can MOT share the number of locals who have joined the industry as bus captains after the introduction of BCM?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Since its inception, the Academy’s focus has been on foundational courses for new bus captains.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: With the conclusion of BSEP, it is unlikely that we would see a large influx of new bus captains in the coming years.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: With the recent launch of the Land Transport Industry Transformation Map (ITM) and the risk of displacement from autonomous vehicles, it is timely that we now cast an eye to the future of the industry.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Are there any plans by the Academy to develop new training programmes focused on upskilling existing bus captains?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: NTWU stands ready to work with our tripartite partners to co-develop programmes to future-proof our bus workers.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: It is imperative that we continue to improve rail reliability to regain the public's trust in our rail system.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: LTA had identified five major upgrading projects to overhaul our ageing MRT lines.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: These are multi-year projects which would extend to 2024.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Can MOT provide an update on the respective major rail improvement projects?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Engineers from the Defence Science and Technology Agency (DSTA) and LTA have recently been seconded to SMRT to bolster its rail reliability regime.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: With the major rail improvement projects ongoing and the construction of new rail lines, such as the Thomson–East Coast Line, does MOT have plans to increase the number of rail engineers and maintenance staff to ensure rail reliability, both in the short and long term?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Are there any plans to work with our schools and Institutes of Higher Learning (IHLs) to ensure that we have enough rail engineers for the future?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: To facilitate the rail upgrading works and allow for longer maintenance hours, we have implemented shortened train operating hours on stipulated days.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: This has benefited our rail engineers and maintenance staff.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Can MOT provide an update on the effectiveness of the Early Closure and Late Opening (ECLO) on rail maintenance work?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Would ECLO become a permanent feature in our rail operations moving forward?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: To accommodate ECLO with minimal disruption to the public transport services, public bus drivers have been redeployed to operate shuttle services during ECLO periods.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Are there any plans to hire more bus drivers for such shuttle services?

speaker: The Chairman
text: Miss Cheng, two minutes for both your cuts.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: In return, the rail operators can then focus on providing reliable and well-maintained rail services for commuters.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Under today's fare review framework, the allowable public transport fare adjustment is based on a formula that is pegged to macroeconomic factors, such as core Consumer Price Index (CPI), Wage Index and Energy Index, which track inflationary price changes.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: For the last few years, we have seen significant expansion in the capacity of our public transport network through the introduction of more new buses and trains, bus services and rail lines.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: However, the additional operating costs were clearly not captured in our current fare formula setup.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: As a result, operating costs have increased drastically while fares have lagged behind for the last few years.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: This needs to be urgently addressed for a more sustainable public transport system and to prevent an increasing burden on taxpayers.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: With regard to this, I would like to understand why fare decreases were granted, despite significant operating cost increases for the last three years?

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Mr Chairman, in 2013, the Land Transport Masterplan visualised a people-centred land transport system by 2030 and to have 75% of all peak-hour journeys to be made on public transport.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Are we on track to meet this target as of 2017?

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Will the Ministry be able to give a breakdown of the mode share distribution of our train, bus, taxi and private hire cars in 2017?

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: What is the likely breakdown by the different public transportation mode come 2030?

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The Transport Minister also recently unveiled the Land Transport ITM where we will leverage emerging technologies to deliver a transport system that is safe, efficient, reliable and comfortable for commuters.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: One such technology is autonomous vehicle (AV) which has great potential to change the way we commute.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Is the Ministry able to assess what is the estimated share by AV, come 2030?

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: With the implementation of AV and with a possible larger presence by 2030, what is the number of workers who may be potentially displaced?

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: What are the targeted and transition measures to help those at risk?

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Currently, we have approximately about 70,000 active drivers.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: To help them cope with potential disruption by AV, I have two suggestions.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This serves to help them make an informed decision on what to expect before joining this sector and not hastily change jobs to become a chauffeur-ride service driver.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I hope that LTA will work quickly with the industry partners, stakeholders and the union to cater enough lead time to help taxi and private hire drivers, who are likely to be impacted, to acquire new vocational skills to transit into a new sector or a new role within the land transport industry.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye
text: Mr Chairman, the transport landscape of today is one characterised by innovation and disruption.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye
text: The recent years have seen the introduction of private hire vehicles and bicycle-sharing, both of which have disrupted the sector considerably.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye
text: In the not-too-distant future, AV technology is set to do the same.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye
text: In the past two years, LTA has initiated several AV trials with various companies.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye
text: How ready are we to implement AVs by 2022?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye
text: Do we have the required infrastructure and the trained workforce?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye
text: Will we have the necessary legislative framework to deal with an accident involving an AV?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye
text: Singapore is not alone in the "race" to develop and deploy AVs.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye
text: Has the Ministry done any studies on the development and use of AVs in other countries?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye
text: What are the experiences and challenges faced by cities which have similarly embarked on AVs?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye
text: With AVs, individuals who depend on driving as a livelihood will be affected.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye
text: Bus captains and taxi drivers, including private hire vehicle drivers, will be displaced by driverless technology.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye
text: Many of them do not have much working experience outside of driving.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye
text: How can we ensure a proper and smooth transition for these drivers?

speaker: Mr Lee Yi Shyan (East Coast)
text: Mr Chairman, Mercer Consulting, which ranked Singapore as having the Highest Quality of Living 2017 has this to say about Singapore: "Singapore’s highly efficient and super-fast public transport is world famous.

speaker: Mr Lee Yi Shyan (East Coast)
text: The MRT has 106 stations and is the second-oldest metro system in Southeast Asia".

speaker: Mr Lee Yi Shyan (East Coast)
text: Train to a city is like an elevator to a skyscraper.

speaker: Mr Lee Yi Shyan (East Coast)
text: It joins discrete spaces and makes them valuable.

speaker: Mr Lee Yi Shyan (East Coast)
text: International recognition notwithstanding, we cannot rest on our laurels.

speaker: Mr Lee Yi Shyan (East Coast)
text: Besides rail infrastructure, we have also improved bus connectivity.

speaker: Mr Lee Yi Shyan (East Coast)
text: At the national level, we have big plans for Changi Airport Terminal 5 (T5) and the Mega Port in Tuas, which will cost tens of billions of dollars to complete.

speaker: Mr Lee Yi Shyan (East Coast)
text: With MOT investing heavily into these transport infrastructure, would the Ministry consider using investments to catalyse the industry development in transport technologies?

speaker: Mr Lee Yi Shyan (East Coast)
text: Does the Ministry foresee our private and public sector building new industry capabilities in engineering, design and system integration along the way?

speaker: Mr Lee Yi Shyan (East Coast)
text: How does the Ministry plan to co-develop the various technologies with the private sector in support of Smart Mobility 2030 vision?

speaker: Mr Lee Yi Shyan (East Coast)
text: How would the Ministry encourage Singapore entities to capture the intellectual property created, so that we can monetise them and invest in our future?

speaker: Mr Lee Yi Shyan (East Coast)
text: Does MOT see the need to champion research and development (R&D) activities in intelligent transport technology?

speaker: Mr Lee Yi Shyan (East Coast)
text: Would the Ministry consider organising more conferences to showcase future transport technologies and advanced prototypes in support of a smarter transport workforce and population?

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Chairman, recently, Changi Airport announced that it is expected to charge travellers and airlines more to fund the Changi East Project, which includes the new Terminal 5 (T5).

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: A bulk of this – $10.80 – comes from the Airport Development Levy.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: While the International Air Transport Association (IATA) has expressed its disagreement with the move, other airports, including Hong Kong, Dubai and Qatar have also done the same for expansion projects.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: However, the Incheon Airport expansion was done without having to raise charges.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Therefore, this raises the question of whether it is possible to optimise our expenditure on the new airport, while still keeping to the required international standards and expectations of Changi.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: If we do have to increase passenger fees, can we not do it in a differentiated way whereby long-haul passengers end up paying more than regional passengers?

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: That way, we do not have to lose our competitiveness as a regional hub.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: The impending demise of the A380 fleet that has previously heralded the long-haul hub-and-spoke model of air travel is under threat.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: So, perhaps Changi Airport should focus more on consolidating its position as a regional hub.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: The Changi East Project is expected to also require funding out of the Government Budget for several years.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: According to MOT and CAAS, the Government will cover the bulk of the project cost and has already contributed about $9 billion to it.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Though the agencies have ruled out borrowing to finance the entire cost of the project, the Changi Airport Group (CAG) and airport users are expected to help shoulder the financial burden of the project so as to help balance the future burden on taxpayers.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: With these updates, it will be useful for the Ministry to update us on the projected costs of the new T5 and how much more of these costs will come from Government coffers.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: In addition, can the Ministry also update us on what alternative means of funding it plans to undertake?

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Will the Ministry consider raising funds or bonds in the private market?

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Why is the Government funding a major part of the expenditure, rather than leave it to Temasek Holdings to fund it from the private market?

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: Drones are popular for recreation and work purposes.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: The former provides an exciting opportunity for amateurs to take pictures from a bird's eye view while the latter provides new business opportunities.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: However, CAAS has imposed many rules and restrictions to make it quite impossible for drones to take off, thereby limiting many exciting opportunities.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: I have two suggestions for MOT to consider.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: This would encourage the use of drones for R&D in these tertiary and research institutions.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: This would help to promote interest in drones in a safe and controlled environment and, maybe one day, we can produce the "Bill Gates of drones".

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: Worldwide, people are coming up with new ways in which drones can be used.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: In the United Kingdom (UK), drones inspect bridges for safety, saving thousands of pounds.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: United Parcel Service (UPS) has started using drones for residential deliveries.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: British Telecoms (BT) has been experimenting with using drones to provide temporary Internet coverage to battlefields, disaster zones and hard-to-reach areas.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: Even drone taxis, which can carry passengers, are in the works.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee
text: Chairman, the advent of third-party ride booking apps has transformed our chauffeured ride services and the way many of us travel.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee
text: When I previously sought for LTA to regulate the third-party ride booking apps operators, LTA had selected a light-touch approach.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee
text: As the popularity of private hire car services grows, they are fast becoming a major part of our public transport landscape.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee
text: Once an operator establishes a dominant market position, commuters may potentially have to bear with higher costs when they are left with limited choices.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee
text: Drivers, on the other hand, may be compelled to follow any terms and conditions set by the operators or risk losing their livelihood.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee
text: Information, such as the safety and condition of their vehicle fleet, should also be submitted to LTA to enhance road worthiness and also to provide protection for the personal data of commuters and drivers.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee
text: We must avoid an over-supply situation and a "churn" mentality among the operators if the numbers are not managed.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee
text: Currently, the taxi fleet is subjected to an annual growth rate if they meet the Taxi Availability indicators.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee
text: Perhaps we can adopt a similar approach for private hire vehicles.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Mr Chairman, I declare my interest as a shipping lawyer.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The Straits of Singapore is one of the busiest waterways in the world.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This figure does not include major incidents involving the loss of lives, pollution or navigational safety.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I am concerned whether the regularity of such incidents will lead some industry players to regard Singapore as an unsafe port, thereby affecting our port's reputation.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Is the Government taking any measures to enhance safety and reduce the number of maritime casualties?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: To improve navigational safety for all vessels, I would like to propose three changes for the current Vessel Traffic Separation Scheme (TSS) in operation in the Singapore Strait.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: One, ban crossings over the TSS for ships leaving or intending to enter the Port of Singapore from or to the Straits.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Vessels should be required to make U-turns at either ends of the TSS at (a) South of East Johor Straits and (b) South of Tuas to access the desired directional lane of the TSS or to enter our port waters or anchorages.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Without ships cutting across the two directional lanes of the TSS, traffic flow and safety will be enhanced.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Two, review the locations of pilot stations around our port waters or consider reducing its numbers to minimise the risk of ships drifting while lying in or near the TSS awaiting pilot boarding.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Three, require all ships to install and switch on their Automatic Identification System (AIS) while transiting the Singapore Strait.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Such vessels should include wooden ships as well as naval and other government vessels, some of which may not currently be doing so.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: AIS helps to identify a ship's call-sign, speed and course of vessel which will assist navigators in all ships in the vicinity to avoid collisions.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Naval vessels often do not switch on their AIS.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: But in the interest of the safety of the many vessels passing through this busy waterway every day, there is a case to reconsider this.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: If military vehicles using a busy highway are expected to follow all road safety rules, why should naval vessels be any different?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Congestion at the TSS or anchorages increases the risks of casualties.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The consequences of any oil pollution resulting from a maritime casualty can be even more damaging.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We should strive to enhance the safety of the Straits and minimise the risks of any casualties.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We may have to initiate discussions at the International Maritime Organization level for some of the measures I have suggested.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: But it will be worthwhile doing this in the interest of safety of lives at sea and the reputation of our port.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee
text: Singapore's position as the leading port in the world has been constantly challenged by the rise of China and rapid developments in China.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee
text: For instance, Shanghai port is far busier than Singapore's port.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee
text: China is also making aggressive moves to build ports in Southeast Asia under its Belt and Road Initiative to reshape trade across Asia.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee
text: China is planning to build an 873-kilometre (km) high-speed rail linking China directly to Thailand's port, and plans are in the pipeline to build a 135-km Kra canal across southern Thailand which would allow ships to bypass the Strait of Malacca and Singapore.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee
text: In Malaysia, China is funding the construction of the East Coast Rail Line (ECRL) under its Belt and Road initiative.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee
text: ECRL will connect ports on the east and west coasts of Peninsular Malaysia and that may alter the current regional trade routes, which ply between the busy Straits of Malacca, passing by Singapore before reaching the South China Sea.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee
text: How is the Government working with PSA to fight such fierce competition fuelled by the Belt and Road initiative so that the new Tuas Mega Port will be our competitive advantage, rather than a white elephant?

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee
text: How could the Government consolidate our position, renew our strategies and innovate, taking advantage of digital and other emerging technologies?

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee
text: Are the existing maritime workers and companies prepared for possible technological disruption?

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee
text: How will the Government help local maritime companies adapt and take advantage of the digital transformation?

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Thus, a resident who does not live near a bus stop or an MRT station can now pick a bicycle near his home and ride to the nearest bus stop or MRT station and thereafter continue with his journey via public transport.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Unfortunately, despite the convenience, the lack of infrastructure planning by the Bicycle Sharing Operators (BSOs) has resulted in much public unhappiness about the bicycle sharing scheme.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: During my dialogues with residents of the private estates, I received so many complaints about bicycles that are parked in a haphazard manner and which obstruct others.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Residents complain about bicycles which are left just outside their homes; bicycles left outside the gate of the condo; bicycles strewn in the middle of the footpath, left at HDB void decks, by the grass verge and so on.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: When I drive, I can even see bicycles lying by the slip road next to expressways and I wonder where was the cyclist going to in the middle of the expressway.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: This is akin to bicycle rental stations in other countries where there is a fixed spot to rent a bicycle.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: The current advantage of the current bicycle sharing scheme is the ability to find a bicycle almost anywhere, as compared to the systems in Europe, Taiwan and other countries where cyclists must walk to a bicycle rental station to rent a bicycle.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: So, if a rider wishes to pick a bicycle from outside his home and ride to the nearest bus stop or MRT station, how will the BSOs provide adequate parking places?

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Will it be that they will provide a parking place for the bicycles next to the condo, next to the bus stop or next to the MRT station?

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: If there are insufficient parking places, does this mean that the riders may still dump their bicycles all over the footpath or by the roadside?

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Just look at the photographs in The Straits Times today showing the bicycles strewn all over the place.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Who shall be responsible for the costs of providing the parking places?

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: There is no compelling reason why the Government should be put to expense for providing parking places or for drawing yellow boxes for the parking of rented bicycles.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: This will ensure that the hirer has an incentive to park the bicycle properly.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Further, if the hirer of the bicycle dumps the bicycle in an indiscriminate manner, or obstructing others, I would urge LTA to work with the BSOs to identify the hirer and thereafter prosecute the hirer for illegal dumping of bicycles.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Judging by the unhappiness raised by members of the public, I urge LTA to implement the new regulations to curb the illegal and inconsiderate parking of bicycles quickly.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: This is a time to show that the Government is responsive to feedback on a matter which has adversely affected many residents.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: It appears that in our rush to accommodate bicycles and PMDs, we have somewhat sacrificed the safety of pedestrians.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: I often hear feedback about cyclists committing hit-and-run.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: I have said it before and I will say it again – without licensing and plating of bikes and PMDs, we cannot identify the culprits.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Besides the mindset of our bicycle and PMD users, infrastructure plays a role.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: When I went to Copenhagen, I saw dedicated cycling lanes parallel to the roads.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: They are often on both sides of the road, so cyclists only move in one direction following the flow of traffic.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: The Copenhagen way also enables cyclists to go quite fast, making cycling a more attractive option.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: There are proper stop signs and zebra crossings where the cycling lane intersects with footpaths.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: In Singapore, we seem very resistant to provide such crossings.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: I have been asking for such a crossing at the exit of Naval Base Primary School where residents have often expressed the concern of their children the moment they step out of the school gate.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: We have on-road cycling lanes on Tanah Merah Coast Road.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: If not, then in many places, pavements need to be widened and segmented.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Is there a plan to do this fast?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Another area we should look into quickly and, I stress, quickly, is the eyesore caused by bike-sharing schemes.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: The bikes are indiscriminately strewn just about anywhere.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: I feel that a penalty should be imposed on the users and bike companies for such acts.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: I have been told that a blind resident fell because his white cane got entangled among the pile of bicycles!

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: In areas where these bikes cause congestion like near MRT stations, perhaps a mechanised parking system for bikes should be built and paid for by the bike companies.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: A word of caution, some bike-sharing companies have already gone bust overseas, leaving their bikes all over the place.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: These bike companies should be licensed and all these undesirable outcomes should be addressed before licences are issued.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: I have even heard of people giving up their daily walks because they are scared of bikes and PMDs.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: For these pedestrians, the dream of a car-lite Singapore has become a nightmare.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: I hope we get our infrastructure, regulations and mindsets right, so that a car-lite Singapore will be realised, not as a nightmare, but as a beautiful dream.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Mr Chairman, Sir, with better free access and more linkways built, we find more PMDs and bicycles being used on our pedestrian walkways.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: However, the width of these walkways has now been increased and pedestrians are annoyed at the inconsiderate use of bicycles or PMDs which speed past them or ring the bells at them when overtaking, as Member Er Dr Lee Bee Wah has just mentioned earlier.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: There have also been many instances where these have resulted in close brushes or accidental hits on pedestrians as they try to speed past the morning or evening crowd.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: While LTA has promoted the use of PMDs and bicycles in our towns, the expansion of walkways and bicycle-ready pathways has not progressed as quickly.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: When we have them, we must make the bicycles and PMDs use them and restrict the use of normal pedestrian walkways when the alternative is available.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Some residents have also expressed concern that the speed limit on PMDs may be fine for an open walkway, but perhaps it is less safe for pedestrians on a narrow footpath with people trying to get to and from work.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Furthermore, the emergence of bicycle-sharing apps has compounded the issue of indiscriminate parking of shared bicycles as many choose to leave bicycles along walkways, shelters and almost anywhere near residential estates and town centres.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: I support LTA's car-lite strategy, but it needs to do more to pre-empt issues by these alternative modes of transportation.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: In addition, I would also say that infrastructure needs to be a priority, especially for heavily utilised pedestrian routes in our estates.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Can the Ministry share with us its strategy to better balance pedestrians, cyclists and PMD user experience?

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Would LTA rework the specifications of all major pedestrian walkways to enable special lanes for PMDs and bicycles?

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: In addition, can LTA share the effectiveness of its education and enforcement efforts on inconsiderate users and accidents involving PMDs and bicycles with pedestrians?

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: As we move towards a car-lite society, it is important that we also pay attention to the alternative modes of transport and how they can support this vision.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: It has been the long-standing wish of residents in Hume and, on behalf of the GRC, they also hope that the Ministry will consider opening the station.

speaker: The Chairman
text: Mr Png Eng Huat, you can take your three cuts.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: What is really new about dockless bike sharing is the proliferation of indiscriminate bike parking.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: These shared bicycles are usually parked haphazardly at void decks, footpaths, lift lobbies, stairways, and I saw two of them parked in the middle of Nicoll Highway yesterday.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: The amount of fines collected from BSOs for not clearing their illegally parked bicycles and the number of bicycles impounded by LTA, as reported in the news last month, is probably just the tip of the iceberg, due to the lack of resources to monitor the indiscriminate parking and to enforce the fine.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: I am not sure if geofencing for bike sharing is in operation already but, from the looks of it, I doubt it is.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: It just confines the problem to a designated area, and the boundary is not even accurate.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: Geofencing may just turn into geo-dumping over time as the designated area would be flooded with shared bikes, causing severe congestion and safety concerns, especially for elderly residents.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: Adding a quick response (QR) code to complement geofencing is an improvement, but such codes can be easily copied with a camera and printer, and you will have a list of parking stations to scan on demand to end your trip even if you are not at the designated parking lot.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: A quick search on the Internet for bike sharing services around the world shows that most existing operations in big cities like New York, Melbourne and Paris all come with docking stations.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: While I do hope the proposed licensing framework would help to rein in indiscriminate bike parking, I am concerned that geo-dumping would be the next big headache for bike sharing services.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: I hope LTA can share more on this because dockless bike sharing has turned Singapore into one giant bicycle parking lot.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: PMDs allow users, usually with no mobility issues, to zip from one place to another faster.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: Some owners of PMDs even use them to piggyback their children from schools, bus stops or train stations.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: PMAs, on the other hand, allow our elderly Singaporeans to get out of their homes to eat, shop or just watch the world go by.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: It allows them to continue to do the simple activities of community living, without which, they may be confined to their homes.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: In short, PMAs allow our elderly citizens with mobility issues a better quality of life.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: I am seeing more PMAs in my estate now.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: However, moving about in a PMA can be challenging on existing footpaths.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: All of them are larger than PMDs and they move a lot slower.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: The footpaths along the roads are certainly not PMA-friendly.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: I had seen some PMAs moving precariously close to the edge of some busy footpaths and I was worried they may tip over.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: The footpaths from the nearest bus stops, train stations, hawker centres, suburban malls, neighbourhood centres and so on, to the nearest Housing and Development Board (HDB) block or private estate need to be widened soon to accommodate these mobility aids.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: I also urge LTA to do another round of initiatives to mop up those remaining spots with barriers so that PMA users can have a smoother connection on our footpaths.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: Last, I also hope LTA could initiate a whole-of-Government approach to accommodate PMAs in our society which, in my view, have given our elderly a fresh breath of life in their sunset years.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: Traffic lights are supposed to give all road users a sense of order, safety and security.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: Our children are taught from young by their parents and in schools to wait for the green-man signal to come on before they can cross the road.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: When the lights are in your favour, it must surely mean it is safe to cross.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: But as it turns out, this is not a given, depending on the traffic junctions you are at.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: This presumption of safety is lost when signalised junctions are programmed with shared green time.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: Such junctions allow vehicles to turn when there are no pedestrians crossing during the green-man phase.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: This, according to the Minister, is to ensure smoother traffic flow on our roads.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: Although the Ministry did not have the breakdown of whether these accidents happened at what type of junctions, 90% of our signalised junctions are programmed with shared green time.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: I am sure there are many unreported near misses as well.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: Last October, LTA was reported to be taking steps to make such signalised junctions safer after some pedestrians were involved in vehicles knocking down the pedestrians who had the right of way came to light.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: There were two cases cited in the news, one of which was fatal.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: It was reported that the fatal accident happened at a signalised junction with shared green time.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: Not only are pedestrians not protected at such junctions, they may also be assigned 15% blame, as a Court of Appeal ruling in 2016 had shown, even though the lights were in their favour.

speaker: The Chairman
text: Miss Cheng, you can do your two cuts.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui
text: It has been more than a year since bike-sharing firms started.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui
text: Over the year, we have seen many cases of shared bikes indiscriminately parked.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui
text: However, with the setting up of more designated bike parking zones near bus stops and drop-off points, this has improved.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui
text: In anticipation of more bike-sharing companies setting up here and a larger bike fleet size from existing incumbents, it leads to a concern whether there will be sufficient designated bike parking places.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui
text: (In Mandarin):   Last month, the AMAP appointed by the Government suggested that electronic scooters be registered with LTA, just like electronic bicycles.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui
text: Recently, there has been an increase in the number of accidents allegedly involving PMDs.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui
text: PMDs, especially e-scooters, make it convenient for users to commute.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui
text: However, when PMDs travel at high speeds, they pose dangers to pedestrians.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui
text: Some PMD users are also reckless and have little regard for the safety of other road users.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui
text: Nevertheless, I believe that most PMD users are responsible.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui
text: They are, therefore, concerned that the registration process would be inconvenient and incur extra costs for them.

speaker: The Chairman
text: Mr Ang Wei Neng, you can do both your cuts.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng
text: Chairman, it is quite rare that both sides of the House are united on one issue.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng
text: That is, speak up against the negative externalities of bike-sharing schemes and the use of PMDs.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng
text: And I want to add another step on this issue as well.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng
text: During my house visits, a sizeable number of residents have related horrific experiences with irresponsible PMD users.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng
text: There were many near-misses and, in some cases, there were injuries and the injuries were quite serious.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng
text: In one case, one of my residents' toes were fractured by a passing e-scooter in the Chinese Garden.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng
text: The user of the e-scooter was in uniform and was wearing a big bag belonging to a food delivery company.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng
text: There were closed-circuit television (CCTV) cameras in the area and this resident made a complaint to the company that provides food delivery, made a Police report and also requested the National Parks Board (NParks) for the CCTV images.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng
text: This could be the tip of the iceberg.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng
text: I think the Parking Places (Amendment) Bill which also seeks to regulate e-scooters is a step in the right direction.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng
text: Sheltered walkways linking neighbourhoods to MRT stations and other transport nodes are well-received by the residents.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng
text: More are walking to the MRT station instead of taking shuttle service or feeder buses.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng
text: However, many residents feel that certain shelters built by LTA are under-utilised.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng
text: On the contrary, other paths leading to transport nodes are well-used by residents but do not have shelter despite repeated requests by the residents.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng
text: LTA's reluctance to build the shelter is because it is slightly out of scope based on its internal guidelines.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng
text: Another example of inflexibility is with regard to the choice of passenger overhead bridges (POBs) where LTA chooses to build a passenger lift.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng
text: In Jurong, LTA has decided to build a lift at the POB nearest to the Chinese Garden MRT station, although that bridge itself is under-utilised as compared to another POB that is slightly further away.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng
text: The bridge that is further away is very well-utilised because it is connected to a town centre.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng
text: For this case, I hope LTA could consider installing a lift at the POB that is more popular with the residents.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng
text: More importantly, I hope LTA can make an effort to consult more with the residents and the community before deciding which POB to build the lift.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng
text: And when it adds more sheltered walkways, they should also consult the residents more.

speaker: The Chairman
text: Mr Yee Chia Hsing, take both your cuts together.

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Chairman, many residents have complained to me that users of bike-sharing services were parking their bicycles in an indiscriminate manner after using them.

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Chairman, I have received a lot of feedback both from residents and personal friends that they know of people who have been knocked down by e-scooter users on pedestrian footpaths.

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Usually such e-scooter users are young and do not stop to render any assistance and just speed off.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong
text: However, inconsiderate or reckless usage of e-scooters and its illegal use on roads have continued.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong
text: Many elderly folks are terrified of sharing walkways with them.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong
text: Enforcement efforts by the authorities were stepped up last year.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong
text: We read of publicity of e-scooters being impounded for illegal use on roads or illegal e-bikes being impounded.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong
text: We see many banners hung on streetlamps highlighting the PMD ban on roads.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong
text: To be fair, the increase in enforcement against errant e-scooter users is a step in the right direction.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong
text: If insufficient efforts are rendered at this stage, we will have a long-term problem of illegal, reckless and inconsiderate usage.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong
text: Our cycling culture is a case in point.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong
text: In my speech during the Second Reading of the Active Mobility Bill, I highlighted the legacy of the lack of enforcement against errant cyclists.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong
text: Today, we can still see cyclists riding against the traffic or not stopping at red lights on a daily basis.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong
text: Timely and consistent enforcement is important as it sets the boundaries for human behaviour.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong
text: In developed countries like the Netherlands and the UK, cyclists comply with cycling rules not because they fear a fine but they grew up learning how to put on the right behaviour.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong
text: We have a problem with our riding culture here, first with cycling, then with e-bikes and now with PMDs.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong
text: The lack of political will for enforcement and to create a right cycling culture in our earlier years has made it much harder for us now.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong
text: In the past year, the problem has been compounded by the popularity of bike sharing.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong
text: Enforcement alone without education is insufficient to change our riding culture.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong
text: But we can do more, as much of the existing efforts are voluntary, not prescriptive, and their reach is limited even if targeted at certain classes of cyclists.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong
text: I shared with this House previously that as a university student in England, I cycled on a pavement once and got roundly told off by an old lady.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong
text: The next generation will grow up knowing what is right and acceptable.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong
text: The course should cover all basic rules and etiquette governing the use of bicycles, electric bikes and PMDs.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong
text: Basic road traffic rules applicable to cyclists, PMD users and pedestrians should also be taught.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong
text: This course can be split up over different age groups over time.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong
text: For example, start with an introductory course for preschoolers and have subsequent courses in early and late primary school levels.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong
text: If a young child can learn to keep left on a skate scooter while riding along the footpath in the park or slow down and give way to an elderly auntie passing by, over time, it will help to engender the right cycling culture in the long run.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong
text: Do this for all types, not just PMDs.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong
text: When everyone knows the rights and wrongs, more people will refrain from wrongful or inconsiderate usage.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong
text: It may help to identify users and facilitate enforcement and, hence, better accountability.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong
text: However, it alone will not resolve existing problems with our riding culture.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: Mr Chairman, clear and strict rules govern driving and more can be done to improve driving behaviour.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: At the same time, we should reconsider the regulations guiding the use of bicycles and PMDs as well as the enforcement of those rules.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: In particular, Sir, we should examine if the interaction of cyclists and PMD users with other road users is a cause for concern.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: I have witnessed groups of cyclists cycling on pavements as well as against the flow of traffic, sometimes alternating between the two.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: I have also seen PMD users on roads regularly.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: Drivers often give way to these two groups of users.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: Often, cyclists and PMD users appear very suddenly and seem incapable or unwilling to brake in time.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: Some of our pavements are clearly unsuitable for PMD and cyclist use.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: When such users navigate narrow pathways, they often switch between the road and pavement.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: When users of bicycles and PMDs do not appear to follow traffic rules for either vehicles or pedestrians and switch between the roads and pavements at high speed, other road users are at least inconvenienced, at worst endangered.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: What are the definitions of dangerous use of bicycles and PMDs that the Ministry bases enforcement on?

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: Are there rules that determine whether a cyclist or PMD rider who switches from roads to pedestrian walk has right of way against pedestrians?

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: What are the rules or guidelines for groups of riders on pedestrian walkways or pavements?

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: What are the rules governing use of electronic devices by cyclists and PMD riders?

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: I urge the Ministry to explore forward-looking approaches to addressing what is the appropriate way to share use of our public spaces.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: The move towards to a car-lite society cannot be used to justify indiscriminate use of alternatives.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: If there are clearer rules for responsible cycling and use of PMDs, it will encourage healthier lifestyles by everyone, including those who do not cycle and use PMDs but still prefer to have a safe stroll on our pedestrian walkways.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: We are all road users, pedestrians or cyclists.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: Why is the minority allowed to define the low standards of public behaviour we witness so regularly these days?

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Will AMAP be reviewing its earlier recommendations in order to tighten the approach towards active mobility device usage?

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: If so, when will the review be completed?

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Apart from rules and code of conduct, will AMAP also be reviewing the insurance and compensation framework for active mobility device usage?

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Another possibility is to set up a fund similar to that set up by the Motor Insurers Bureau for accident victims who are not protected by third-party insurance.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Chairman, Sir, I join many of my colleagues who spoke before me about the proliferation of bicycles and PMDs.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: I am actually standing here to speak even though I have lost my voice because I promised my residents that I will speak for them.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Many important points have already been highlighted by my colleagues, including the nightmare that hon Member Er Dr Lee Bee Wah shared.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: My residents, too, have nightmares with cyclists and PMDs.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: So, I would not repeat the long list of things that I intend to speak on.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: But what other measures can the Government take to facilitate a safer and more pleasant shared use of our public spaces between pedestrians and riders?

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: And how can errant cyclists and PMD riders be dealt with promptly?

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee
text: Chairman, by 2030, the total number of elderly Singaporeans will increase to 900,000.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee
text: The Silver Zone programme, started in 2014, is one good initiative.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee
text: To date, eight silver zones spread across the island have been completed.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee
text: Can we speed up the projects' implementation so that more mature estates with a large number of elderly residents, such as Ang Mo Kio Town, can have safer roads for senior users?

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee
text: I have two hawker centres and markets in Cheng San Seletar and many elderly residents will benefit from early adoption of the silver zone in this area.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: Mr Chairman, our excellent connections to the world provide huge advantages for our businesses, create good jobs for Singaporeans and raise our quality of life.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: They make Singapore a global city and a vibrant economic hub.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: The role played by Changi Airport and PSA is well-understood.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: As the Chinese saying goes, "一 山 还 有 一 山 高".

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: Many airports and seaports in the region are working hard to replace us.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: Changi Airport and PSA are working even harder to make sure we are not easily replaceable.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: The Ministry of Transport (MOT) is fully behind them, together with other Government agencies.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: That is why we are expanding Changi Airport, even though we have just opened Terminal 4 (T4).

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: By adjoining the current airport, it will almost double our overall airport capacity.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: More importantly, we can synergise both airports to make the entire Changi an unbeatable air hub.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: But more than physical size, the new seaport will leverage the latest technology and help create new innovative solutions.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: As the operator of the new seaport, this will set PSA apart from its rivals.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: It will help make PSA’s customers even more efficient and cost-effective in their operations.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: While the external connectivity dimensions of Changi Airport and the seaport are obvious, the role played by land transport is also crucial.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: No point being able to fly or sail into Singapore easily, only to be stuck in traffic jams.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: This is a common phenomenon in many other cities around the world.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: The key is to ensure our land transport matches the standard of Changi and PSA.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: Our approach is to make public transport the preferred mode of transport within Singapore.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: As Mr Sitoh Yih Pin put it, there will be growing pains, but I am confident we will get there.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: We are on track to achieve this target.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: With the introduction and growing popularity of personal mobility devices (PMDs), we can be increasingly confident.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: We are clear that for public transport to be the preferred mode, it must be extensive, affordable, reliable and seamless.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: A well-connected and resilient rail network forms the backbone.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: Eight in 10 households will live within a 10-minute walk of a train station by 2030.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: That is why we are expanding our rail network to 360 kilometres (km).

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: We will also increase the number of stations to 270.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: This will put our rail network density ahead of Tokyo and New York City today.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: This is hard work, patient work over many years and several Transport Ministers.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: When we fully opened the Downtown Line last year, we took a giant step forward.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: The next giant step will be the opening of the Thomson-East Coast Line.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: We have also started planning the Jurong Region Line and Cross Island Line.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: These new Mass Rapid Transit (MRT) lines will help to catalyse the development of the Jurong Lake District and Punggol Digital District and transform them to enable an exciting car-lite lifestyle for more Singaporeans.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: Besides the MRT, we have also enhanced bus services significantly, as noted by Mr Melvin Yong.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: Through the Bus Contracting Model, we have raised service standards by injecting additional capacity for more than 100 services.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: To support the expansion of our bus fleet, four new depots as well as seven interchanges and terminals have been built or upgraded over the past five years.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: We have also incorporated an incentive-disincentive framework in the bus contracts.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: For the first service year, the operators have already earned incentives of about 1.5% of their total service fees.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: This is nearly $20 million of incentive payment.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: The more they improve their services to commuters, the more incentives they stand to gain.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: This has aligned their corporate objectives with ours.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: Together, these measures have contributed to greater bus connectivity, less crowded rides and shorter waiting time for commuters.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: It showed up in the Public Transport Customer Satisfaction Survey.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: I see this as a vote of confidence by commuters for BSEP and the new Bus Contracting Model.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: To measure affordability, we track the percentage of income that lower-income Singaporeans spend on public transport.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: In other words, out of your monthly salary, how much do you spend on public transport?

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: So, if you earn $1,000, less than $20 is spent on public transport.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: While transport fares must be affordable, we must be careful that they are not priced too cheaply, as maintaining a high-quality transport system requires resources.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: Cheap fares are popular, but they are not sustainable.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: The story of the New York City subway is instructive.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: A recent New York Times article, reproduced in our local media, which chronicled the woes of the New York City subway.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: The investments we are making to improve the transport system are huge.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: MOT’s budget is now the second biggest amongst Ministries, after the Ministry of Defence (MINDEF), and ahead of the Ministry of Health (MOH), the Ministry of National Development (MND) and the Ministry of Education (MOE).

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: Miss Cheng Li Hui has observed an alarming spike in public transport subsidies.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: She knows that rising cost against declining revenue has only one outcome – a disaster.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: One major contributing factor is the huge increase in network capacity as we opened new lines and added more buses and trains.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: This huge cost increase has been borne by the Government, namely, taxpayers.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: Against such rising cost, fares have gone down by 2% over the same period.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: So, 60% rise in operating costs but fees reduced by 2%.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: The Government will continue to subsidise public transport to keep fares affordable.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: However, every dollar spent on transport is a dollar less for other expenditure, like schools, healthcare and security.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: The Public Transport Council (PTC) is currently reviewing the fare formula, and I agree with Miss Cheng Li Hui that the current formula is inadequate.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: It can be improved to better track total costs.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: I am confident that they can work out a fair and sustainable arrangement.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: Please support the PTC when they make their recommendations.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: Meanwhile, we need to be prudent about where and when to inject new services, especially in low ridership areas, so as to not overburden taxpayers.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: I hear Mr Zaqy Mohamad’s call, on behalf of Mayor Low Yen Ling, for better rail connectivity in Bukit Gombak.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: Mayor Low is a good Member of Parliament (MP).

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: I have to be a good Transport Minister.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: I have to balance the needs of all Singaporeans in a fair manner.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: We are committed to opening Hume MRT station eventually.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: But the exact timing of this will depend on the pace of developments and ridership growth in the area.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: We do not need the story of the New York City subway to remind us of the importance of reliability.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: The Singapore Mass Rapid Transit (SMRT) has its own bad experience of past neglect and, hence, its fair share of reliability problems in recent years.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: But we will get there; we just need time.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: I asked for five years when I took over this portfolio two and a half years ago.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: That is why very few metros in the world have achieved that.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: After a painful 2017, the new signalling system in the North-South Line has finally stabilised.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: I am pleased to report that the MKBF of the MRT network, for January and February this year, has exceeded next year’s target of 600,000 train-kilometres.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: In fact, the North-South Line hopes to cross its 150th consecutive day of no disruption today.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: The bad news is that we will soon start testing of the new signalling system on the East-West Line with passengers.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: We have been testing it without passengers; that means, at midnight.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: We will soon be testing it with passengers on board.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: I will be spending many days and nights briefing the MPs along this stretch of East-West Line to explain to them what re-signalling is all about, why we need to re-signal, why it is good for Singapore and the commuters and what to expect, especially the unpleasant experience of the North-South Line.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: Extended engineering hours have been very useful to our engineering team.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: They allow us to speed up the renewal of ageing assets, as well as the installation of noise-barriers around the island.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: For residents living next to MRT tracks, this is a welcome development – my residents as well as residents of Er Dr Lee Bee Wah.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: Extended engineering hours have also allowed us to step up preventive maintenance and repairs.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: To answer Miss Cheng Li Hui’s question, we require our rail operators to fulfil stringent Maintenance Performance Standards (MPS).

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: If they fail to comply, we will impose regulatory action and financial penalties.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: More importantly, after several years of interacting with them, my sense is that our two rail operators themselves have already internalised the importance of maintenance and they have accepted their responsibility to regain public confidence in our MRT system.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: I am optimistic they will not fail us.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: They are ramping up the number of maintenance staff.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: Over the past five years, our maintenance workforce has grown by over 1,500 staff, a 50% increase, with plans to further increase this by more than 600 over the next three years.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: To answer Mr Melvin Yong’s question, ECLO will continue, especially for the older lines where we have to juggle limited engineering time between maintenance and the renewal of ageing systems.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
