text: We have learnt to manage such planned closures with an extensive shuttle bus arrangement so that affected commuters have convenient travel options.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: During the recent planned closures along the entire East-West Line, we mobilised 350 buses and 700 bus captains to support the shuttle services.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: Many readily adjusted their work schedules to accommodate the additional works.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: During one Sunday closure, this was in December, along the North-South and East-West Lines, many members of SMRT's track circuit replacement team were unable to attend the wedding of their teammate, Mr Mohammed Idris bin Zakaria.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: The team managed to send him a photo and message from the worksite, which read: "Hi Idris, we are working at Jurong due to ECLO, hot sun and rain are a big challenge here.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: In fact, it is going to rain, but we know today is your big day, we all just want to say, Happy Marriage".

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: We are determined to make our system among the best in the world.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: Until all the ageing assets are fully replaced and upgraded, we may still encounter some delays or disruptions.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: But we are doing our best to eliminate such risks and, should they happen, to minimise inconvenience to commuters.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: They were ordered to meet growing ridership demand and to replace our ageing bus fleet.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: We are opportunistically bringing forward their purchase and deployment to strengthen the resilience of our public transport network in the interim.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: Like Mr Melvin Yong, we, too, are concerned about staff fatigue.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: Planned closures are generally over the weekends, when bus services are thinner, so we have been able to tap on the existing pool of bus captains for these shuttle services.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: To manage driver fatigue, bus captains are rostered to ensure that they have sufficient rest.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: We will continue to work closely with the public bus operators and National Transport Workers' Union (NTWU) to ensure that such shuttle services are sustainable, and that we maintain strong morale amongst our bus captains.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: Besides our oldest MRT Lines, enhanced maintenance and renewals are also underway for all the other MRT and Light Rail Transit (LRT) lines, which are at different stages of their lives.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: The Bukit Panjang LRT, in particular, is reaching the end of its useful life.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: Bukit Panjang residents can look forward to more reliable rides in due course.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: Commuter perception of public transport is often shaped by their first- and last-mile experience.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: We are helping pedestrians by providing more covered walkways to transport nodes.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: Shared bicycles and PMDs have also provided commuters with a new option for shorter journeys.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: However, disamenities, specifically indiscriminate parking and reckless behaviour, are a growing irritation.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: I remember Mr Sitoh Yih Pin's reservations on e-bikes and PMDs when the Act was debated in this House last year.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: This year, I noticed, out of the 33 cuts for MOT, 14 were on shared bicycles and PMDs.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: Yesterday evening, I heard all the passionate pleas from the Members who spoke.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: So many spoke, including Ms Foo Mee Har, despite her loss of voice.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: I heard such complaints from my wife, too.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: Every time when she drives around our estate and sees such yellow, rainbow-coloured bicycles parked indiscriminately, blocking the footpaths, believe me, I would get an earful.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: So, clearly this is a hot topic among many people on the ground!

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: Senior Minister of State Lam Pin Min will address this topic in full later.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: I hear Mr Pritam Singh's call to significantly tweak the Certificate of Entitlement (COE) system to favour families with young children and also low-income motorcyclists.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: COE is a sound market-based mechanism to allocate limited vehicle supply.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: Favouring one specific group would inevitably disadvantage others.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: Meanwhile, we are committed to making public transport the preferred mode for all Singaporeans.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: This applies not just for new families, but also for the elderly and persons with disabilities.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: Senior Minister of State Lam Pin Min will also elaborate on this later on.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: We also facilitate the introduction of car-sharing services, such as BlueSG, and welcome the growth of private hire car services.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: They have provided commuters with more on-demand and point-to-point alternatives to owning a car.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: How it consolidates can have serious implications on contestability and the welfare of commuters and drivers.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: In other words, will the industry remain open and contestable?

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: Today, we have choices between Grab and Uber, and that is why service level improved.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: What if the market consolidates and you end up with only one player or a very huge dominant player?

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: I am quite sure that pricing will change drastically overnight, both for taxi drivers as well as commuters.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: So, as regulators, we have to anticipate such possible outcomes and try to pre-empt them.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: Second Minister Ng Chee Meng will discuss this very important issue later on.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: Emerging technologies are unsettling, but the opportunities to transform land transport for the better are compelling.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: The ITM will help the industry and its workers move up the value chain and serve commuters in new and better ways.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: Mr Melvin Yong and Mr Ang Hin Kee spoke about Autonomous Vehicles (AVs).

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: AVs have the potential to transform transport, reinvent transport.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: We are working with some of the best in the world and in Singapore to tap on this exciting technology which is still developing.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: We are keenly watching where this technology will take us next and the benefits that it will bring to commuters.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: It is too early to say how widely adopted AV technology will be by 2030, but the progress of AV trials overseas and in Singapore is very encouraging.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: Waymo of Google has tested their AVs on public roads in the United States (US) without a safety driver.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: This is what we call Level 4 or 5 of a driverless vehicle.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: It intends to launch a commercial AV ride-sharing service later this year.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: Here in Singapore, we expanded our AV testbed at one-north last year to about 70 km.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: Mr Melvin Yong asked if we have the necessary infrastructure and legislative framework.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: We have also launched a Request for Information to seek inputs from industry and other experts.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: This week's Economist magazine had a special report on AVs.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: Several pages of this developing technology are worth a quick flip through.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: It spells out possibilities, an exciting world of transport.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: Singapore was mentioned in the article as an example of pro-innovation regulation.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: It is so easy to snuff out innovation.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: If you regulate too tightly, too early, nothing will happen.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: If you maintain a light touch for too long, as has happened in the bike-sharing situation, then you have disamenities.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: This reminded me of what Laozi said 2,500 years ago on the art of frying a small fish: too much fire and you burn the fish.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: Too little fire, the fish remains uncooked and you may get a stomachache.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: Although it is difficult to predict the timing of widespread AV adoption, the potential for such technologies to disrupt the livelihoods of transport workers is undeniable.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: I, therefore, agree with Mr Melvin Yong and Mr Ang Hin Kee that we should help our transport workers adapt early.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: The Government is working closely with unions and the transport operators to upskill, reskill and to transition some of them to adjacent vocations.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: This is being done through our Institutes of Higher Learning (IHLs), as well as the Bus Academy and Singapore Rail Academy.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: We will also work with Government agencies, industry champions and service providers to identify other areas of employment growth outside the land transport industry for affected workers to transition to.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: It will provide our transport workers with a clearer picture of what skills they should develop as well as the programmes available, if they want to upgrade.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: Mr Chairman, the future transport scene is truly exciting.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: We are lucky to be living in Singapore, and at this time.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: For example, AVs, combined with the sharing economy and improvements in mobile telephony, have made on-demand point-to-point transport service a reality.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: And when it comes about, who needs to own a car?

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: If you want to go anywhere, use your mobile phone, call up.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: Why should a car look like a car?

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: Once you have driverless vehicles, there is no need for steering wheel, brakes and pedals, the car does not need to look like a car.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: Some of these autonomous pods in the trials do not look like cars at all.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: And they can be reconfigured very easily to take one passenger or two passengers, if you want greater intimacy.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: Or if you have a family of five children, it can be reconfigured too, much like Hollywood’s transformers.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: This will have a huge impact on city planning.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: The roads and carparks will be freed up.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: Much of the accidents are due to human errors.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: Do flip through the Economist's special report this week to have a glimpse of this brave new world.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: Is it a dream or will it be a nightmare?

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: We can never guarantee how the future will be like.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: But the articles in the Economist's special report offer good advice.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: It is in our hands to shape this future to make sure that it will not be a nightmare; it will be a good dream, provided our policies remain pro-innovation, pro-market and also, very importantly, right pricing of limited resources.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: The quality of life of our children will definitely be better than ours.

speaker: The Second Minister for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Mr Chairman, I thank the MPs for their cuts on aviation and private hire cars (PHCs).

speaker: The Second Minister for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: The air hub is a cornerstone of our economy.

speaker: The Second Minister for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: It contributes significantly to our gross domestic product (GDP) and provides many good jobs.

speaker: The Second Minister for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: The excellent connectivity that our air hub provides also helps to facilitate trade, investments and tourism.

speaker: The Second Minister for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Singaporeans, our businesses and our economy continue to benefit from a strong air hub.

speaker: The Second Minister for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Changi Airport is currently connected to over 400 cities around the world.

speaker: The Second Minister for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: It is well-connected to the three most populous Asian countries, with links to 34 Chinese, 16 Indian and 14 Indonesian cities.

speaker: The Second Minister for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: The number of passengers in the wider Asia Pacific region is also expected to grow from 1.4 billion to 3.5 billion in the next 20 years.

speaker: The Second Minister for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: This is 2.5 times today's number, and more than double the expected passengers in the next biggest region, Europe.

speaker: The Second Minister for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: As air traffic in our region and the world continues to grow, the Government is committed to ensuring that Changi Airport remains best positioned to capture its share of the growth.

speaker: The Second Minister for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: And in the coming years, traffic growth is expected to be at 3% to 4% annually.

speaker: The Second Minister for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: To ensure that Changi Airport has sufficient capacity to capture this growing demand, we need to enhance our airport infrastructure.

speaker: The Second Minister for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: We have successfully built up a strong air hub over the last 30 years, in large part due to our bold and forward-thinking approach to anticipate our future needs.

speaker: The Second Minister for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Some Members in the House might recall that the Government decided to build Terminal 2 (T2) in 1975, even before we moved our airport from Paya Lebar to Changi.

speaker: The Second Minister for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: This was 15 years before its opening in 1990.

speaker: The Second Minister for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: We then made plans for a new Terminal, T3, and decided to build it in 1996.

speaker: The Second Minister for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: When we opened T3 in 2008, Changi Airport was serving close to 38 million passengers and, at that time, there were some who wondered if we needed such a large increase in capacity.

speaker: The Second Minister for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Today, we have almost fully utilised all the 66 million passengers per annum (mppa) capacity across Terminals 1 to 3.

speaker: The Second Minister for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: If we had not built T4 in good time, Changi Airport would have reached its maximum capacity in two years.

speaker: The Second Minister for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: It will also further enhance the passenger experience by providing a wide range of new retail and dining offerings in what would be Singapore's largest indoor garden to come.

speaker: The Second Minister for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Our long-standing approach of building ahead of demand has served us well.

speaker: The Second Minister for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: It has allowed Changi Airport to consistently deliver a high standard of service to passengers, even during the peak hours.

speaker: The Second Minister for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: This "Changi Experience" is what distinguishes Changi from all other airports around the world.

speaker: The Second Minister for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: We have, therefore, adopted a similar approach in planning and building T5.

speaker: The Second Minister for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: T5 is an integral part of our airport expansion at Changi East.

speaker: The Second Minister for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: It is a bold move to firmly cement Changi Airport's position as a premier air hub for the future.

speaker: The Second Minister for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Air connectivity is a key link for Singapore.

speaker: The Second Minister for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: It is critical that our aviation sector can continue to grow and support the growing needs of our economy.

speaker: The Second Minister for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: As Minister Khaw said earlier, building Changi T5 is not just building another new terminal; it is akin to constructing a second airport.

speaker: The Second Minister for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Our airport expansion thus far has largely consisted of the construction of new terminals.

speaker: The Second Minister for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: But the Changi East project goes far beyond the terminal building itself.

speaker: The Second Minister for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Extensive land preparation and drainage works at Changi East have been ongoing since 2014.

speaker: The Second Minister for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: The works for a three-runway system have commenced since 2016.

speaker: The Second Minister for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: We are extending an existing military runway and constructing a network of taxiways to allow for Changi Airport to cater to more flights.

speaker: The Second Minister for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: If we actually laid out the runway and taxiways in a long line, it would stretch from Changi Airport all the way to Tuas, almost as long as the Pan Island Expressway (PIE) of 42 km!

speaker: The Second Minister for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Next comes a network of tunnels and systems, including a baggage handling system and automated people-mover system.

speaker: The Second Minister for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: These will allow for the efficient transfer of passengers, baggage and airside vehicles within Changi East itself, and also between Changi East and the existing Terminals 1 to 4.

speaker: The Second Minister for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Last but not least, is the T5 terminal itself.

speaker: The Second Minister for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: This will be a mega terminal with satellite terminals.

speaker: The Second Minister for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: It will allow Changi Airport to serve up to an additional 50 mppa in its initial phase.

speaker: The Second Minister for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Fifty mppa is a 60% increase from Changi's current capacity and is more than the combined capacities of Terminals 2 and 3.

speaker: The Second Minister for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: T5 will allow better integration of airport operations, improving their efficiency as it allows us to pool resources.

speaker: The Second Minister for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: It will benefit passengers like you and me by offering quicker access to boarding gates and convenient transfers.

speaker: The Second Minister for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: The "Changi Experience" will be further enhanced and new standards for passenger experience will be set.

speaker: The Second Minister for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Mr Zaqy Mohamad raised a pertinent question about the cost and funding of T5.

speaker: The Second Minister for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: The entire Changi East project is expected to cost tens of billions of dollars.

speaker: The Second Minister for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: The Government will invest substantially in Changi East and foot the majority of the costs.

speaker: The Second Minister for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Airlines and passengers will also need to contribute towards enhancing this airport infrastructure.

speaker: The Second Minister for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Currently, airlines and passengers pay various aeronautical charges to CAG.

speaker: The Second Minister for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Some have questioned why we are increasing the charges now when T5 will only be completed around 2030.

speaker: The Second Minister for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: As I have explained, Changi East is not just about Terminal 5.

speaker: The Second Minister for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: It is a massive project with many phases.

speaker: The Second Minister for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Airport users will start to benefit from Changi East progressively.

speaker: The Second Minister for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Having users start paying earlier will also avoid large spikes in the amount they have to pay later on.

speaker: The Second Minister for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: We have, indeed, considered it, but decided on our current option, which is a flat rate, regardless of the distance travelled.

speaker: The Second Minister for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Passengers use the same facilities at the airport, regardless of where they are flying to.

speaker: The Second Minister for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: So, it is only fair that the charges that they pay are the same.

speaker: The Second Minister for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: This is the same principle that has been used for other passenger charges, such as the Aviation Levy and the Passenger Service and Security Fees.

speaker: The Second Minister for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Mr Zaqy Mohamad also asked why the Government is funding the majority share of the project.

speaker: The Second Minister for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Changi Airport is vital to Singapore's economy and connects us to the world.

speaker: The Second Minister for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: It yields significant economic benefits for Singapore beyond the airport directly and the aviation industry.

speaker: The Second Minister for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: By funding Changi East, the Government is making a strategic investment into Singapore's future.

speaker: The Second Minister for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Without Government funding, airport charges will have to increase much more.

speaker: The Second Minister for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Given the importance of the air hub to Singapore, we need to strike the right balance and keep charges for airlines and passengers at a level that will ensure that Changi remains competitive and continues to be the air hub of choice.

speaker: The Second Minister for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Mr Zaqy Mohamad also highlighted the example of Seoul’s Incheon Airport.

speaker: The Second Minister for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: When comparing the costs of that airport expansion, we need to take into account the difference in scale and complexity of each project.

speaker: The Second Minister for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: The Government will ensure prudent spending on Changi East.

speaker: The Second Minister for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: The project will deliver good value for money.

speaker: The Second Minister for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: We have thoroughly analysed the traffic projections for Changi.

speaker: The Second Minister for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: We are also carefully scrutinising the cost of Changi East.

speaker: The Second Minister for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: We will strive for the most cost-effective way to develop Changi East and ensure that Changi continues to be world-class.

speaker: The Second Minister for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: In developing Changi East, we are building for the long term.

speaker: The Second Minister for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: This is a major investment, to meet our future needs and reap benefits for Singapore and Singaporeans in the long run.

speaker: The Second Minister for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: CAG is in the midst of evaluating proposals from three consortiums bidding to be the Master Building Consultant for T5.

speaker: The Second Minister for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: The three consortiums have all submitted designs that will set T5 apart from other airports around the world.

speaker: The Second Minister for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: I am confident that Singaporeans will be proud of our new T5 when it is completed around 2030.

speaker: The Second Minister for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Mr Chairman, we are at an exciting time in Singapore's transport history.

speaker: The Second Minister for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Besides Changi East, we are also building the new mega port at Tuas, the High Speed Rail and Rapid Transit System connecting us to Malaysia, as well as extending our MRT network.

speaker: The Second Minister for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: These enhancements and investments will enhance our transport infrastructure and bring with them a multitude of benefits.

speaker: The Second Minister for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: First, Singaporeans will enjoy the direct benefits of greater convenience and access in their travel around the island and to other parts of the world.

speaker: The Second Minister for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Second, local enterprises and their workers will have valuable opportunities to gain new expertise and enhance their capabilities.

speaker: The Second Minister for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: As highlighted by Mr Lee, our transport infrastructure investments create new and exciting possibilities for our businesses.

speaker: The Second Minister for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Singapore businesses have the opportunity to work on complex projects which, in some cases, are of an unprecedented scale.

speaker: The Second Minister for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Many of our transport projects, in fact, have stringent and unique requirements for which they need to apply innovative solutions.

speaker: The Second Minister for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: For example, a joint venture formed by our local companies Hock Lian Seng Infrastructure and Sembcorp Design and Construction are working on a part of the three-runway system under the Changi East development project.

speaker: The Second Minister for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: The works involve extensive aircraft pavement and drainage works.

speaker: The Second Minister for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: On the maritime side, SurbanaJurong is the engineering design and construction supervision consultant for Tuas Terminal and has taken the opportunity to apply many innovative engineering solutions in the planning and construction process.

speaker: The Second Minister for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Our companies will gain valuable expertise and knowledge, deepen their experience and burnish their credentials from working on these and other projects.

speaker: The Second Minister for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: In fact, a number of projects and initiatives that the Government is supporting will result in the creation of valuable intellectual property (IP).

speaker: The Second Minister for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Where there is IP created as a result of such projects, companies would typically have the rights to use the IP for their commercial purposes.

speaker: The Second Minister for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: And we encourage them to do so, including to develop exportable solutions, to seize opportunities abroad, especially as Asia's demand for infrastructure and transport solutions grow.

speaker: The Second Minister for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: One example is Singapore Technologies Kinetics (STK), which has partnered MOT and LTA to develop autonomous buses and shuttles.

speaker: The Second Minister for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: I hope that, one day, we can see STK-developed AVs driving around in other cities.

speaker: The Second Minister for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: The Government will continue to champion research and development (R&D) in the transport sector to ensure that local capabilities continue to grow and are showcased globally.

speaker: The Second Minister for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: There are already many such opportunities, such as the Singapore Airshow, the Singapore Maritime Week, and the Singapore International Transport Congress and Exhibition.

speaker: The Second Minister for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: As Mr Lee also highlighted, the Government can spur industry development and the growth of the transport sector by championing R&D and working with industry players to develop new technologies and adopt innovative processes.

speaker: The Second Minister for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: In air transport, there are two areas of focus to leverage technology developments.

speaker: The Second Minister for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: The first is airport operations, and the second is in the area of unmanned aircraft systems (UAS) or drones.

speaker: The Second Minister for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: First, let me touch on leveraging technology for airport operations.

speaker: The Second Minister for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Passengers using T4 today will be familiar with some of the new technologies, such as the use of facial recognition to get passengers from the kerbside to the plane in a speedy fashion.

speaker: The Second Minister for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Advanced computed tomography (CT) X-ray machines have also been deployed at T4, which do not require passengers to remove their laptops from their bags during security checks.

speaker: The Second Minister for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: These are examples of the suite of Fast and Seamless Travel (FAST) self-service options which we have already tapped on to create a better, smoother and more seamless travel experience for those using Changi Airport.

speaker: The Second Minister for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: We are also excited about the possibilities of using such technologies to change the way we work.

speaker: The Second Minister for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: By automating the routine processes, we free up workers’ time to focus on areas where the human touch cannot be replaced.

speaker: The Second Minister for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: For example, passenger service agents at T4 now do not stay behind the counter.

speaker: The Second Minister for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: They feel more fulfilled, contributing in more meaningful ways.

speaker: The Second Minister for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: This has reaffirmed their commitment to continue working as a part of the Changi Airport community.

speaker: The Second Minister for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: The Government is prepared to collaborate with industry to spur further adoption of technology.

speaker: The Second Minister for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: For example, Singapore Airlines (SIA) launched its Digital Innovation Blueprint programme in January this year, in collaboration with the Agency for Science, Technology and Research (A*STAR), the Civil Aviation Authority of Singapore (CAAS), the Economic Development Board (EDB) and the National University of Singapore (NUS).

speaker: The Second Minister for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: SIA aims to set up a Digital Innovation Lab and tap on data analytics to further enhance customer experience as well as boost the operational efficiency of its aircraft maintenance processes.

speaker: The Second Minister for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: This is an example of how the Government’s partnership with industry can help support companies and their staff in their digitalisation efforts, so that they can bring service standards to even higher levels.

speaker: The Second Minister for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: The Government will also invest significant resources into developing innovative processes and technologies to entrench Changi as the world-class hub it is today.

speaker: The Second Minister for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: ATP will not only level up the system capabilities of our air hub but also ensure that our workers remain at the forefront of their fields.

speaker: The Second Minister for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: For example, as air traffic volume grows, our air traffic controllers (ATCOs) will have a more challenging job.

speaker: The Second Minister for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: We will, therefore, leverage technology to further enhance our Air Traffic Management (ATM) capabilities.

speaker: The Second Minister for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: This will provide our ATCOs with a wider range of tools to do their job well and ensure that Singapore remains a leading Air Navigation Services Provider in our region.

speaker: The Second Minister for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: As we tap on advancements in technology to manage our skies, the ATCO's job will also evolve and require deeper skills and a wider range of expertise.

speaker: The Second Minister for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: They will even participate in the development of advanced software and hardware that are more sophisticated than those available today.

speaker: The Second Minister for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: The new scheme will allow ATCOs to progress to higher grades, compared to the past.

speaker: The Second Minister for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: By providing more avenues for progression and targeted professional development based on the aptitude and interest of each ATCO, the new ATCO scheme of service will further professionalise the job of the ATCOs.

speaker: The Second Minister for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: It will also deepen their expertise and allow us to develop a pool of ATCO professionals who will help to drive CAAS up the ATM value chain.

speaker: The Second Minister for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: The levelling up of capabilities of workers in our air transport sector is part of the vision we set out to achieve through the Air Transport ITM.

speaker: The Second Minister for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: This will serve as a reference for those who are already in the sector or for those wanting to join the aviation industry.

speaker: The Second Minister for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: It is paramount for us to support workers in the air transport sector to continually retrain and upgrade themselves, even as we leverage more advanced technologies to improve the sector's productivity.

speaker: The Second Minister for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: We want our air transport workers to be able to manoeuvre technological changes at the workplace to their advantage and take on new roles that will challenge and fulfil them even more.

speaker: The Second Minister for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: This will also allow them to add greater value to their jobs and their companies and, overall, to our economy.

speaker: The Second Minister for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: The second key technological development in the air transport sector is the unmanned aircraft systems (UAS).

speaker: The Second Minister for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Today, UASes are already being deployed for tasks, such as worksite inspections, surveying and mapping, improving processes and saving time and manpower.

speaker: The Second Minister for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: There is huge potential for UAS to spur new and innovative applications across industries.

speaker: The Second Minister for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: This would further increase productivity and enhance service delivery.

speaker: The Second Minister for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: One such area is in logistics, where UAS can quickly deliver parcels by air to the end-consumer.

speaker: The Second Minister for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: In time to come, UAS can potentially even ferry people through the air, adding a new dimension to urban mobility.

speaker: The Second Minister for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: At the same time, we recognise that UAS operations could pose concerns about safety and security.

speaker: The Second Minister for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: These concerns must be addressed before the full potential of UAS can be realised.

speaker: The Second Minister for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: In particular, given Singapore’s busy airspace and dense urban environment, we need to be extra careful that UASes do not pose risks to manned aircraft operations or public safety.

speaker: The Second Minister for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: The Government, having said all that, has been pushing the boundaries in exploring UAS in our urban environment so as to seize the potential benefits that the use of UAS could bring.

speaker: The Second Minister for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: For instance, LTA is trialling the use of UAS to perform rail and road tunnel inspections with greater ease and accuracy.

speaker: The Second Minister for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: In addition, LTA has also deployed UAS at selected Thomson East-Coast Line worksites to help our engineers monitor construction progress and identify defects.

speaker: The Second Minister for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: We are, indeed, excited about the drone estate’s potential to spur more R&D on UAS technologies and foster meaningful commercial partnerships.

speaker: The Second Minister for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: We intend to progressively expand the scope and scale of the UAS activities there, bearing in mind that we must do so responsibly and not compromise safety.

speaker: The Second Minister for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Recreation UAS flying may take a while longer.

speaker: The Second Minister for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Mr Chairman, let me now turn to how technology has transformed the point-to-point (P2P) industry.

speaker: The Second Minister for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: The introduction of third-party booking apps and PHC services has revolutionised the P2P industry in Singapore.

speaker: The Second Minister for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: The matching of demand and supply is also enhanced through the platforms and through dynamic pricing.

speaker: The Second Minister for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Complaints about taxi unavailability, which were prevalent before, have also come down significantly.

speaker: The Second Minister for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Taxi drivers, who were initially affected, are now starting to reap some of the benefits, too.

speaker: The Second Minister for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Taxi companies are offering more flexible rental schemes, lower rental rates and more choices of service platforms to drive for.

speaker: The Second Minister for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Additional booking channels have also given taxi drivers an additional revenue stream and have helped reduce empty plying of roads.

speaker: The Second Minister for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Mr Luen is a GrabTaxi driver currently driving for SMRT.

speaker: The Second Minister for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: He likes that there are multiple rental schemes now that he can pick from.

speaker: The Second Minister for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: While he is currently paying a daily rental for his taxi, he is looking to switch to an hourly rental scheme which may better suit his needs.

speaker: The Second Minister for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: At the same time, I also note that there is some concern on how taxi and PHC drivers could be impacted by technology changes.

speaker: The Second Minister for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: We will also explore having modules in the Taxi Driver’s Vocational Licence and the PHC Driver’s Vocational Licence courses to help equip taxi and PHC drivers with digital skills, such as using navigational apps.

speaker: The Second Minister for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: We had decided a few years ago, when the PHC industry was still in its early stages of development, to impose minimal conditions on PHC booking service operators.

speaker: The Second Minister for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: This is to avoid stifling innovation in the then nascent industry.

speaker: The Second Minister for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: This is why the current regulatory regime for PHCs focuses primarily on protecting commuter safety and interests via licensing of PHC drivers and PHCs.

speaker: The Second Minister for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: The PHC booking service operators are required to dispatch only licensed drivers and cars.

speaker: The Second Minister for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: However, since then, the PHC sector has grown and changed the P2P industry significantly.

speaker: The Second Minister for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: From an emerging fringe transport mode, PHCs have become an important part of our land transport system.

speaker: The Second Minister for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: The PHC industry has evolved and consolidated rapidly.

speaker: The Second Minister for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: There are currently two large players – Grab and Uber.

speaker: The Second Minister for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Both companies allow taxis to use their booking services, which blurs the lines between the PHC and taxi industries.

speaker: The Second Minister for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Mr Ang Hin Kee asked whether the Government will be reviewing our regulatory approach for the P2P sector.

speaker: The Second Minister for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: First, the sheer size of the PHC industry means that the actions of PHC booking service operators affect a significant number of commuters and drivers today.

speaker: The Second Minister for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Second, today, there are limitations to our current regulatory regime.

speaker: The Second Minister for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: We only have basic requirements on booking service operators to protect commuter safety.

speaker: The Second Minister for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: In exceptional situations, LTA can issue a suspension order to forbid drivers from driving for these PHC booking service operators.

speaker: The Second Minister for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: But this is a very blunt tool, which impacts commuters and drivers as well.

speaker: The Second Minister for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Given the growing PHC industry, it is imperative that the Government has sufficient regulatory oversight over the PHC booking service operators to protect the interests of commuters and drivers.

speaker: The Second Minister for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: More details will be made known in due course.

speaker: The Second Minister for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Mr Chairman, MOT is committed to making travel even more convenient and seamless, across our island and beyond, for Singaporeans.

speaker: The Second Minister for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Our efforts to develop Changi East will help to achieve this, as will our investments in more advanced technologies.

speaker: The Second Minister for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: At the same time, we will help our workers to keep up with the changes and have good careers in the transport sector.

speaker: The Second Minister for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: We are confident that besides Singaporeans, Singapore companies will benefit from these efforts, as they harness new productivity gains throughout the entire transport ecosystem.

speaker: The Second Minister for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: We can look forward to a more liveable and well-connected Singapore, supported by robust and effective transport systems.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Mr Chairman, Maritime Singapore is a thriving ecosystem, anchored on our global hub port and vibrant international maritime centre (IMC).

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Singapore's port registered a strong performance in 2017.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Our IMC also performed well and was ranked the world’s top international shipping centre by Baltic-Xinhua for the fourth consecutive time.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: We welcomed new players, such as Ocean Network Express, which will set up its global headquarters in Singapore this April.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Existing players like Maersk, CMA CGM and Thome also expanded their presence in Singapore with the establishment of their new vessel monitoring hubs.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: However, we are mindful that the sector’s landscape is evolving rapidly and remains challenging.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Digitalisation is already transforming global transportation and supply chains, blurring the boundaries between the shipping and logistics sectors.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Emerging technologies, like blockchain, are paving the way for new business models, forcing companies to rethink the way they do business or risk being disintermediated altogether.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Faced with structural problems like slowing trade growth and shipping overcapacity, the outlook for the global maritime sector remains uncertain.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: And as Mr Ang Wei Neng noted, several developments have sparked talk about the emergence of alternative trade routes in the region.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: China is investing in ports and transport infrastructure across Southeast Asia under its Belt and Road Initiative (BRI).

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: These include several ports and the East Coast Rail Line in Malaysia.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Interest in the Kra Canal has also recently surfaced, but it remains uncertain whether it will be built.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: As the region develops, it is inevitable that our port will face greater competition from alternative ports and trade routes.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Thus, while we are well-placed, we cannot be complacent.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: The only way for us to stay ahead is to continue to innovate and look for new growth opportunities.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: For instance, with our strong connectivity, we are in a good position to contribute to and pursue opportunities under BRI.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: In the longer term, the growth in trade and networks in the region will also benefit Singapore.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: To build on our strengths to meet new challenges, we have set out new growth strategies for Singapore’s maritime sector, which are in line with the IMC 2030 Advisory Committee's recommendations to grow Singapore as a "Global Maritime Hub for Connectivity, Innovation and Talent".

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: These strategies will prepare our companies and workers for the future.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: First, we will continue to enhance Singapore’s connectivity.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: This will enable us to remain plugged into the regional and global economy and continue to be relevant as a hub for maritime activity and businesses.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: To boost our physical connectivity, we are investing in long-term port capacity and infrastructure to meet the industry’s needs.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Significant investments, such as in the Next Generation Tuas Port, will ensure that Singapore retains its leading position as a global hub port.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Reclamation works for the first phase of Tuas Terminal are progressing well.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: We will also strengthen our connections to the region to enhance Singapore's position as a key node in the region's maritime network.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: I spoke about how we can pursue opportunities under China’s BRI.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Under the Chongqing Connectivity Initiative, which is the third government-to-government (G2G) project between Singapore and China, we have developed the Southern Transport Corridor (STC), the maritime route linking China’s overland Silk Road Economic Belt and the Maritime Silk Road.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: This will strengthen our position as China's gateway to Southeast Asia and create new opportunities for our local companies to venture overseas.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: We are working on enhancing and growing the STC.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: In fact, many of our companies are already participating in BRI.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: To tap on growing trade from Western China, PSA operates many ports along the BRI, including Qinzhou in the Guangxi-Beibu Gulf, which provides direct access by rail to Chongqing, a gateway to China's vast inland area.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Local shipping line, Pacific International Lines, has similarly invested in logistics facilities in the region and runs shipping routes between the Guangxi-Beibu Gulf and Singapore.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Back home, PSA has also entered into a joint venture with China Ocean Shipping Company (COSCO) Shipping to operate three berths at Pasir Panjang Terminal, which will help bring trade volumes through Singapore.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Building up our physical connectivity alone is not enough.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: We must also build a more interconnected and vibrant network, to be a node for maritime business activities and information flows.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Today, Singapore's IMC is home to over 5,000 establishments and offers a comprehensive range of maritime services.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Looking ahead, we will continue to grow the diversity of our services.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Besides encouraging established companies to venture into new business activities, we will catalyse the growth of non-traditional players.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: These include maritime technology enterprises, such as Alpha Ori and Metcore, and digital platforms like VesselsValue.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: In the longer term, we will explore setting up a port and logistics cluster at Tuas to encourage collaboration and co-innovation with related sectors.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: This will open up new growth areas for our companies and enable us to leverage Singapore’s hub connectivity to enhance our value-capture.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: For example, co-locating logistics firms near the port could spur more efficient supply chain management and allow them to experiment with fresh concepts, such as inter-modal logistics.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Second, we will create a vibrant and innovative maritime sector to help drive industry transformation.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Singapore’s maritime sector is already on the steady pathway of innovation and experimentation.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Mr Lee Yi Shyan asked about our plans to champion R&D in transport technology.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: We will continue to provide an enabling environment for innovation to facilitate the development of smarter solutions.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: MPA’s Living Lab, which was set up last year, aggregates lead user demand and allows for the test-bedding of technologies in real operational conditions.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: These include the development of a remote-assisted pilotage system for harbour pilots to steer vessels from shore, and the testing of vessel traffic management solutions.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Over time, other kinds of industry data will also be shared.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: With this rich information resource, anyone will be able to analyse or even overlay the data with their own datasets, opening up possibilities for the development of new applications, services and products.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Supported by the National Research Foundation (NRF) and MPA, the MTP will co-fund, with matching investments from industry players, the development of technologies with high potential for industry application.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: With its focus on automating and digitalising port and shipping operations, and enhancing maritime safety and security, MTP will be pivotal in driving industry transformation, making our port smarter and safer, and our IMC more competitive.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: To ensure that our companies and workers benefit from the sector’s transformation, we will grow and build the capabilities of local enterprises.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Take, for example, Xjera Labs, a local startup that has ridden on the digitalisation wave to design AI-based solutions for the sector.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: With funding support from MPA, they worked with Jurong Port to develop a proof-of-concept that uses video analytics to automatically track container vehicles at the port.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: With this system, Jurong Port will be able to streamline security checks and improve operational efficiency, resulting in manpower savings of about 15%.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: To give more startups like Xjera Labs a helping hand, MPA will launch the Maritime Technology Acceleration Programme (MTAP) to help startups translate their ideas into marketable solutions.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Under MTAP, promising startups and entrepreneurs will receive tailored mentorship from industry partners, and networking opportunities with potential investors.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: The Government will do its part as a convenor, demand aggregator and facilitator to help catalyse innovation.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: But ultimately, companies must take ownership in rethinking their operations to pursue higher productivity and new opportunities.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: We, therefore, encourage more companies to come on board MPA's schemes and projects under the Sea Transport ITM.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Last but not least, a skilled maritime workforce is critical to meet the needs of the industry and set us apart from our competitors.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: To equip Singaporeans with the necessary skills and experience to take up these good jobs, we will introduce new and enhanced training programmes.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: For those who aspire to join the sector, MPA's Global Internship Award (GIA) offers students the opportunity to intern with international maritime companies in Singapore and overseas.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: For example, GIA was vital in helping Ms Melisa Yeo decide on embarking on a career in the maritime sector.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: In 2015, she completed a 10-week internship at shipping company Oldendorff, including a two-week stint in Lubeck, Germany.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Melisa enjoyed the experience so much that she joined Oldendorff full-time upon graduation.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: She is now an operations trainee based in Singapore.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Going forward, MPA will be enhancing the GIA to strengthen the relevance of the internship experience, and more details will be released ahead of the next run of the programme.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: For those in the sector, we will help them progress in their careers.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: MPA will roll out a new Global Talent Programme (GTP) to groom Singaporeans for leadership roles in the maritime sector, by offering them opportunities to hone their skills through structured rotations and overseas exposure.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: For seafarers who wish to upgrade themselves beyond their captain or chief engineer positions, MPA will also provide more progression pathways for their sea-to-shore transition.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: More details will be announced later this year.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: The funds will also be used to grow non-traditional players in the maritime space, and support pilot projects to test new business concepts.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: But as we push on with these ambitious plans to grow Singapore as a maritime hub, we cannot neglect the basics.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: To maintain navigational safety, MPA operates the Vessel Traffic Information System (VTIS) to monitor shipping traffic in the waters around Singapore.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: MPA carries out regular enhancements to its VTIS, which was installed in 2011 and upgraded early last year.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: In addition, MPA has built on the International Maritime Organisation's (IMO's) International Convention for the Safety of Life at Sea, and required all vessels, except for government and naval vessels, to turn on their Automatic Identification System (AIS) when calling at our port.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Regulations also play an important role in ensuring safety.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Mr Dennis Tan proposed to ban crossings over the Traffic Separation Scheme (TSS) for ships leaving or entering our port and, instead, require them to make U-turns at the eastern and western ends of Singapore.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: We have looked into this and assessed that it is not that practical.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Vessels that are east-bound via the Straits of Malacca will have to travel all the way to the east of Singapore, make a U-turn before calling at our port.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Moreover, if vessels are only allowed to make U-turns at these two designated areas, it may also result in bunching and congestion, potentially increasing the risk of incidents.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: So, this will affect the efficiency of our port and prevent vessels from proceeding to their next destination expeditiously.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Instead, areas are demarcated within the TSS where vessels, taking necessary precaution, may make their crossing.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Vessels have to play their part in ensuring safety.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: They must also comply with the rules of crossing.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Mr Dennis Tan also suggested that MPA review the location of our pilot boarding grounds to minimise the risk of ships drifting when waiting for pilots.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Most recently, in 2014, MPA worked with the industry to revise the locations of our pilot boarding grounds to reduce the risk of incidents.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: MPA also introduced a scheduling system for vessel arrivals.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: This reduced waiting time for ships and enhanced safety of navigation.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Beyond rules and regulations, we seek to improve the practice of good seamanship and advocate a safety-first culture at sea.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: MPA established the National Maritime Safety at Sea Council in 2015 to drive such efforts.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: MPA also holds safety conferences, workshops and briefings under its Safety@Sea campaign.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: The Third International Safety@Sea Conference will be held in June this year.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Mr Chairman, this is an exciting time for Maritime Singapore.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Our maritime sector is not only growing but transforming fast.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: In the next few years, we expect many rewarding jobs to be created and new growth opportunities to emerge.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: The Government will continue to work closely with our partners so that we stand ready to seize these opportunities and ensure Singapore's continued success as a leading global maritime hub.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: So, even as we create more good jobs and opportunities for our workers and companies, we are also working to enhance the quality of life for all Singaporeans.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Minister Khaw Boon Wan spoke about a more reliable and smarter land transport system.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: I will now share MOT's plans towards a more inclusive and safer land transport system.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Our land transport system should serve all Singaporeans, from the young and mobile, to the elderly, families with young children and persons with disabilities.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: We have made significant strides in our journey towards a more inclusive transport system but there are still areas where we can do better and in making the journeys more comfortable and convenient for Singaporeans from all walks of life.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: We will, therefore, need to continue to make our roads and paths safer for all, not just for the young and active, but also for those who are less mobile.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: We will also need to ensure that our transport system is accessible to all commuters, including those with diverse needs.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: On Mr Png Eng Huat's concern about signalised junctions with shared green time, LTA has adjusted traffic light timings to give pedestrians a headstart in crossing the road, and installed lighted road studs, additional road markings and signs at higher risk junctions to remind motorists to give way.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: We will continue to study the situation and do more where we can.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Mr Ang Hin Kee asked about the progress of Silver Zones.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: As and when the need arises, we will look into providing more Silver Zones.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: We will also strive to make everyone’s journey to public transport more comfortable.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: In 2012, we embarked on the Walk2Ride programme to build a comprehensive network of covered linkways, connecting public transport to nearby developments.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: We have also received feedback from the elderly and persons with disabilities that they have encountered difficulty climbing the stairs of pedestrian overhead bridges in order to cross the road.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: We will extend this programme to about 50 more overhead bridges, starting with those within walking distance from hospitals and polyclinics.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: We will do our best to meet the needs of the less mobile.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: However, we need to prioritise our efforts, given the high costs of about $4 million per pair of lifts.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: In this regard, I would like to reassure Mr Ang Wei Neng that we will be prudent in our efforts, focusing on locations which most benefit those commuters who are less ambulant.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: We also believe that everyone should be able to travel independently on public transport.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: We do acknowledge that the elderly, families with young children, and commuters with disabilities may face some challenges.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: We have, therefore, worked towards building a more inclusive public transport system that caters to all commuters, including those with diverse needs.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Today, all MRT stations and bus interchanges are already barrier-free.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: To facilitate priority boarding for people with special needs, the elderly and families, we have implemented priority queues at 17 MRT stations, seven bus interchanges and two Integrated Transport Hubs.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: We target to extend this initiative to all MRT stations by 2019 and to all bus interchanges and Integrated Transport Hubs by 2021.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: I would also like to take this opportunity to commend our commuters for showing care towards one another.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: At Outram Park MRT Station, the PTC launched the "Heart Zone" and "Heartwheels @ Linkway" initiatives in August 2017.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Commuters who need help getting to Singapore General Hospital can wait at two designated areas for assistance.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Wheelchairs are also provided at both ends of the transfer linkway.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Many commuters have extended a helping hand to those in need, guiding them to their destinations, or pushing the wheelchairs along the linkway.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: I am very heartened by the success of these initiatives.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: We will continue to explore innovative solutions to help commuters with disabilities.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Last year, we shared LTA’s plan to collaborate with SG Enable to "adopt" Redhill Station, to improve the first and last mile between the station and the Enabling Village.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: LTA and SG Enable have, in the past few months, spoken to and followed commuters with special needs on their journeys to understand the pain-points and challenges in their daily commute.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: LTA has since installed rest stops with seats that allow pedestrians to rest, and edge markings along the footpaths to help pedestrians, those with low vision especially.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Students from the Pathlight School also contributed their artistic talent, putting up unique and colourful signages to help direct the way to the Enabling Village.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: LTA will also collaborate with industry partners to develop and pilot assistive technologies for commuters with special needs.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: One of the ideas surfaced is an Assistive Passenger Information System for buses.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: It includes a mobile application that allows special-needs users to notify bus captains of their intention to board.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: For visually impaired passengers, there will be internal and external speakers to announce the service number, destination and the next bus stop.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: It also directly transmits audio announcements via hearing aids to hearing-impaired passengers.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: The trial will start later this year on bus service 139, which serves the Enabling Village.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Earlier, Minister Khaw spoke about the various transport options for families.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: We are also making public transport friendlier for families with young children.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: For example, all new bus interchanges, Integrated Transport Hubs and all interchange stations on the Thomson-East Coast Line will be equipped with nursing rooms.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: In addition, all 35 stations along the Thomson-East Coast Line and Circle Line 6 will have family-friendly washrooms, with diaper changing stations, child-size toilets and barrier-free facilities.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: At the Committee of Supply (COS) last year, we announced that we would start allowing families to board public buses with open strollers from 2 April 2017.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: We have received positive feedback from families that these initiatives have made their journeys more convenient.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Some commuters have also given feedback that there may not always be sufficient room for more than one open stroller or wheelchair.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: All these efforts will make getting around more convenient for families, without the need to own a car.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: We will continue to listen to commuters' suggestions to make further improvements.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: My Parliamentary colleague Mr Sitoh Yih Pin, Chairman of the Government Parliamentary Committee for Transport, and Mr Richard Magnus, Chairman of PTC, are leading a Panel to gather feedback and will be making recommendations on how we can make our public transport system more family friendly.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: The Panel comprises diverse members, from academics to parents with young children.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: We look forward to hearing their recommendations in the middle of this year.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: We will continue to push our boundaries and explore creative solutions to make our environment safer and more accessible to all.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: The growing use of bicycles and PMDs has made first- and last-mile journeys more convenient for many commuters.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Dockless bicycle sharing services have also made active mobility more accessible and affordable.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: I agree with Mr Zaqy Mohamad and Er Dr Lee Bee Wah that our infrastructure needs to keep up with the increasing prevalence of active mobility.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: When planning our new towns, we will also prioritise the allocation of space to pedestrians, cyclists and PMD users.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: However, the rising popularity of active mobility brings new challenges.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: We have observed a number of fire incidents involving motorised PMDs.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: LTA is working with relevant stakeholders to study imposing more safety requirements on motorised PMDs, in addition to our existing requirements on their weight, size and maximum speed.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: In the meantime, users should exercise caution and purchase compliant PMDs from reputable sources and refrain from modifying their PMDs.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: To deter reckless behaviour, we have enlisted the help of other agencies and community partners in our enforcement and education efforts.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Since May 2016, LTA has issued over 3,000 advisories for unsafe riding on paths.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: The National Parks Board (NParks) rangers and the Traffic Police officers have also stepped up their patrols in parks, on park connectors and on roads.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: About 900 volunteers from the grassroots are patrolling their neighbourhoods to educate cyclists and PMD users on safe and gracious behaviour.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: We thank these enforcement officers and volunteers for their tireless efforts to keep our paths safe.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: In February 2018, LTA also rolled out the Safe Riding Programme.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: To address Assoc Prof Randolph Tan's concerns, the programme will educate cyclists and PMD users about the appropriate use of our active mobility infrastructure, and safe and considerate behaviour when sharing paths with others.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: I agree with Mr Dennis Tan that we need to build a right culture for safe riding.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: And as Mr Dennis Tan suggested, we are already working with schools to educate students about the key active mobility rules and safe riding practices.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: We will also require cyclists and PMD users caught riding recklessly to attend this programme.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Despite our efforts to educate and encourage safe riding practices, Mr Sitoh Yih Pin, Mr Ang Wei Neng, Mr Yee Chia Hsing, Miss Cheng Li Hui, Ms Foo Mee Har and Ms Joan Pereira have shared their concern about the number of accidents involving bicycles and PMDs.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan had also pointed out the danger of PMDs being used on roads.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: I agree totally with Members that inconsiderate cyclists and PMD users not only endanger themselves, but also pedestrians and road users, and this is very worrying.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: We have zero tolerance for reckless behaviour and will further tighten up our enforcement efforts.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: We recently enhanced the penalties for PMD users caught riding on roads.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: They may face a composition sum of up to $500 for the first offence.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Those who ride on expressways will not be offered composition and will be charged in Court.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: If convicted, they will be liable to a fine of up to $2,000 and/or imprisonment of up to three months for the first offence.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Last month, the Active Mobility Advisory Panel recommended the introduction of a registration regime for e-scooters.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: The Active Mobility Advisory Panel will also take a deeper look at our active mobility rules.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Ms Joan Pereira, Mr Zaqy Mohamad, Mr Yee Chia Hsing and Er Dr Lee Bee Wah have given us valuable suggestions for the Panel to look into, such as reviewing the speed limit on footpaths, and the insurance and compensation framework.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: The Panel will look into these issues, weighing the need for these initiatives against the impact on the large majority of responsible users and taking into account the practices of other jurisdictions.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: The Panel will publish its recommendations by the end of this year.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Our tough stance targets the minority of reckless users to deter bad behaviour.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: It should not discourage the majority of responsible and considerate users from enjoying the benefits of active mobility.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: With a safer environment, the benefits of active mobility far outweigh the obstacles we are facing.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Next, let me move on to addressing Members' concerns over the indiscriminate parking of dockless shared bicycles.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Many Members, including Er Dr Lee Bee Wah, Miss Cheng Li Hui, Mr Png Eng Huat, Mr Yee Chia Hsing, Ms Foo Mee Har, Mr Zaqy Mohamad and Mr Lim Biow Chuan have spoken on this issue very passionately.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: These bicycles obstruct other commuters and cause clutter in community spaces.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: It is the responsibility of every shared bicycle user to park their bicycles appropriately in bicycle racks or designated bicycle parking zones, which are widely available at all MRT stations and housing estates.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Over the past year, LTA has stepped up efforts to address the problem.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: In October last year, LTA, Town Councils and NParks signed a Memorandum of Understanding (MOU) with the bicycle sharing operators.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: It sets out guidelines for responsible operation in public spaces.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: We have also enforced strictly against indiscriminately parked bicycles.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Unfortunately, the problem of indiscriminate bicycle parking persists.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: This Bill will enable LTA to regulate the bicycle sharing operators through a licensing framework.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: First, LTA will be able to manage the size of each operator's fleet by setting a maximum cap for each operator.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: This is similar to what Miss Cheng Li Hui suggested.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: We will start off conservatively in the first instance.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: If an operator can demonstrate that it is able to manage indiscriminate parking and ensure good utilisation of its fleet, it will be allowed to grow over time.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: This ensures that we start off right and put in place the appropriate incentive structure for operators to proactively manage indiscriminate bicycle parking.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Second, LTA will have stronger levers to ensure operators do their part to manage indiscriminate parking.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Under the proposed licensing regime, we can impose standards and conditions, for example, to require operators to remove indiscriminately parked bicycles within a stipulated period.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: These penalties are higher than the $500 per bicycle fine we currently impose on operators.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: We also intend to implement Er Dr Lee Bee Wah's suggestion of requiring licensed operators to provide a security deposit.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
